chunk_findings.detail: The bullet “`--full` (MCP `full=true`) lifts every cap for that call” is unconditional, but the `allow_full` knob description below says `allow_full=false` makes `--full` still return the capped answer. In an org layer or local config where `allow_full` is set to `false`, a user reading this line will expect `ddflow next --full` (or the MCP equivalent `full=true`) to return the uncapped list, while the actual behavior is a capped list with an explanatory note. The bullet should qualify that `--full` lifts caps only when `allow_full` is true.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/output-caps.md:10

chunk_findings.detail: The changed assertion now requires the truncation message for a `--json status` invocation to contain `ddflow status --full`, which drops the `--json` flag. The command that produced `body` in this test is `run_cli(repo, "--json", "status")`, so the named next call is not an equivalent rerun: a JSON consumer following it gets non-JSON output. This violates [R-audit-ux], which requires refusals/truncations to name the next call; the next call must preserve the invoked format (e.g. `ddflow --json status --full` or `ddflow status --full --json`).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_status_bound.py:60

chunk_findings.detail: The bullet at line 10 states that `--full` “lifts every cap for that call,” but the knob table at line 23 states that when `allow_full=false`, `--full` still returns the capped answer. In an org-lock environment with `allow_full=false`, running `ddflow next --full` will not lift the cap, so the advertised behavior is false for that configuration, and the footer’s suggested “everything: `ddflow next --full`” next call would not actually produce full output.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/output-caps.md:10,23

chunk_findings.detail: The change ships default output caps with non-zero values, so enforcement is active by default for every top-level read command. The change’s own conformance clause in the intent states that “new enforcement ships warn or off.” Here the caps are instead on: a user must explicitly pass `--full` (and have `allow_full=true`) to get unfiltered output. To satisfy the stated constraint, the first shipment should default `max_rows` and `max_chars` to 0 (off) or add a `warn_only` default before enabling truncation.

chunk_findings.detail: The default `max_chars=30000` is justified in the doc as “about 4 characters a token,” which only holds for typical ASCII-like English text. Given a top-level `next` or `status` call on a log whose single row contains 30,000 CJK characters or emoji, the row cap (`max_rows=50`) does not truncate it, and the 30,000-character cap does not truncate it either. Those 30,000 code points commonly tokenize to more than 25,000 tokens (emoji often split into multiple tokens each; CJK is roughly one token per character), so the MCP tool result exceeds the hard 25,000-token cap the change is meant to satisfy. This violates the stated falsifier that every top-level read command stays under 25,000 tokens. The default must be reduced or the guard must use the actual tokenizer rather than a character proxy.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/output.py:20 max_chars

chunk_findings.detail: The new `capflags` module lives in `ddflow.surfaces.declared`, so `from ..registry` resolves to `ddflow.surfaces.registry`, which is not where the declared-surface `Param` class lives; that class is defined in `ddflow.surfaces.declared.registry`. Importing this module (for example, when `ddflow.surfaces.declared.lifecycle.navigate` runs `from ..capflags import capped`) raises `ImportError`/`ModuleNotFoundError` before any capped command can register, so `next` and the new `--full`/`--cursor` flags are broken.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/capflags.py:5

chunk_findings.detail: Run `ddflow recover --plan` on a repo with many recoverable items, without `--full`. The recover command is registered with `*capped(True)`, while board and status use `*capped(False)`. Because `capped`’s positional boolean is the default for the generated `--full` flag, recover gets `full=True` by default, so the later `_cap(..., "recover", a)` sees full output requested and does not bound the triage. That keeps the huge recover output uncapped by default, directly violating the default output cap for recover in D-scope-focus-2026-11 and the 25000-token falsifier.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/reporting.py:recover command `*capped(True)`

chunk_findings.detail: When `ddflow_next` is called with `full=true`, the new early-return branch returns the blocked list untouched while still applying `_lean` to the ready list (`{**body, "ready": [_lean(i) for i in body.get("ready") or []]}`). The normal path below applies the `_lean` projection to blocked items as well. So `full=true` changes the MCP shape of blocked rows: blocked entries no longer get the usual projection, and any internal fields hidden by `_lean` leak into the full MCP response. Example: `ddflow_next(full=true)` on a queue with blocked items returns raw blocked item dictionaries, while the default path returns `_lean`-projected dictionaries; `--full` is supposed to print all rows, not to change each row’s schema.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp_bound.py:bound_next

chunk_findings.detail: When `[output].allow_full=false` and the caller requests `full=True`, `apply` caps the answer and marks the full request as refused, but `_annotate` unconditionally writes `"all": "`ddflow <command> --full` (MCP: `ddflow_<command> full=true`) lists every entry"` into `truncated`. That is false: the named call will be refused and will not list every entry. The refusal metadata therefore names an invalid next call, contrary to the requirement that refusals name the exact next call; an MCP client reading `truncated.all` gets a command that cannot work.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/output_caps.py:_annotate [D-scope-focus-2026-11]

chunk_findings.detail: `_cut_lists` cuts lists under `_render` but does not record those cuts in `info`. In `apply`, after `_fit`, if `not info and not cut_chars and not (start and COMMANDS[command][3])` it returns the original `out`, discarding the `work` dictionary. An outcome whose only oversized list is `_render`—for example `out.data={"text": "ok", "_render": {"items": list(range(100))}}` with `max_rows=15`—is returned unchanged with all 100 `_render` entries, so the row cap has no effect when no top-level list was cut. This defeats the intended cap on `_render`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/output_caps.py:_cut_lists

chunk_findings.detail: The documented `allow_full = false` “org lock” only suppresses the `--full` flag. The same section says `max_rows = 0` and `max_chars = 0` each “lifts” its cap, and that each knob can be set from the local environment. Input: an org config contains only `[output] allow_full = false`; a user runs `DDFLOW_OUTPUT_MAX_ROWS=0 DDFLOW_OUTPUT_MAX_CHARS=0 ddflow next`. Per this documentation, both row and character caps are now lifted without `--full`, so the command returns uncapped output, defeating the claimed org lock. [r-safe-by-default]

chunk_findings.detail: The truncated-next-call assertion now expects `ddflow status --full`. The body this test inspects is produced by `ddflow --json status` (it is parsed with `json.loads` and checked through `body["truncated"]`), so the equivalent CLI rerun command that preserves the caller’s JSON output is `ddflow --json status --full`. Dropping `--json` makes the asserted hint direct the user to a human-readable full status, not the JSON they were just consuming. This either makes the test fail against a correct implementation that preserves flags, or pins an incorrect next-call hint; it violates [r-tell-dont-discover].

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_clip_rows` does not actually guarantee the `budget` because the loop returns on `n == MIN_CLIP` even when `_size(clipped) > budget`. Input: a JSON (`wire=True`) `next` command with the default `max_chars=30000` (so `budget=15000`) and `out.data={"rows": [{"f0": "a"*100, ..., "f199": "a"*100}]}`. `_fit` reduces the list to one row, then `_clip_rows` reaches its floor `n=80`, clips each 100-char field to 87 chars (the ` [...]"` marker adds 7 after the 80 chars), and returns a body of about 17,200 characters — over the 15,000-character JSON budget. The cap therefore does not hold on a single large-ish row requiring no special config.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/output_caps.py:_clip_rows

chunk_findings.detail: `_clip_rows` only calls `_clip_strings` for top-level values that are `list`s (`isinstance(v, list) and not k.startswith("_")`); a top-level `dict` value such as `_render` is left untouched even though `_cut_lists` treats `_render` as output and reports it. Input: `status` with `wire=False` (so `budget=30000`) and `out.data={"_render": {"items": [{"summary": "x"*40000}]}}`. `_clip_rows` never clips the 40,000-character `summary`, records nothing in `info` (so `apply` has no reason to return the `work`), and the original uncapped body is returned, exceeding `max_chars`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/output_caps.py:_clip_rows

chunk_findings.detail: The new hunk only filters `clipped_strings`; the `"all"` footer is still emitted without checking `conf.allow_full`. With `[output] allow_full=false` and a caller passing `full=True`, `apply` correctly refuses the full request, but `truncated` still contains `"all": "ddflow <command> --full (MCP: ddflow_<command> full=true) lists every entry"`. That named call will be refused, so the refusal metadata names an invalid next call, violating [D-scope-focus-2026-11]. The associated test name suggests a fix, but this output_caps.py delta does not change that line.

chunk_findings.detail: The previous invalid-advertisement bug is only fixed for the explicit `full=True` request. With `[output] allow_full = false` and a normal default run of `ddflow next` (no `--full`), `full_refused` is false, so the new `if not full_refused:` guard still inserts `truncated["all"] = "`ddflow next --full` (MCP: `ddflow_next full=true`) lists every entry"`. That call is refused by the org lock, so the metadata/advertisement still names an invalid next call that will not list every entry. The added test only checks `full=True` under `allow_full=false`; it does not cover the no-`--full` default path, so the confirmed defect remains for the standard usage.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/output_caps.py:_annotate

chunk_findings.detail: The implementation in `apply` changes the default fallback for `max_rows` and `max_chars` when `allow_full` is false: `rows = conf.max_rows or (50 if not conf.allow_full else 10**9)` and `chars = conf.max_chars or (30000 if not conf.allow_full else 0)`. If a configuration explicitly sets `max_rows = 0` or `max_chars = 0` under a normal (non-locked) organization, `conf.max_rows` evaluates to falsy, and `0 or (50 if not conf.allow_full else 10**9)` evaluates to `10**9` correctly. However, under `allow_full = false`, `conf.max_rows = 0` evaluates to falsy, and the expression `0 or (50 if not conf.allow_full else 10**9)` evaluates to `50`, so setting `max_rows = 0` is ignored and replaced by the default cap of 50, even though the documentation and the intent state that setting configuration knobs to zero lifts caps.

For a `--json status` caller, the correct next-call CLI form is `ddflow --json status --full`; `ddflow status --full` produces human output, not the JSON list. If `output_caps` generates the correct full JSON call, this test fails; if it generates the asserted string, it violates [r-tell-dont-discover] by not naming a call that preserves the caller’s output format.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_status_bound.py:60

chunk_findings.detail: `status_args` returns `{"full": True}`, which unconditionally forces `full=True` for every `status` invocation regardless of whether the user passed `--full` or not. Given input where a user runs `ddflow status` expecting the default output cap to limit the result size, line 276 overrides it to full output, defeating the scope focus intent where status is capped by default.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/output_caps.py:276

chunk_findings.detail: When `work` already has a `truncated` dict containing an `"all"` key (for example, an outcome that was capped in an earlier pass and is then re-annotated), and the new annotation has `full_refused == true`, the code does `work["truncated"] = {**old, ...}` and only assigns `"all"` when `not full_refused`. It never removes the old `"all"`, so the capped output still advertises the lift that was just refused. The newly added `test_a_refused_lift_does_not_advertise_the_lift_and_zero_knobs_do_not_undo_the_lock` passes a fresh outcome without a pre-existing `"all"`, so it does not catch this stale path.
